name: Hank Williams
hook: An Alabama singer who learned guitar from a Black street musician, wrote the songs country music still measures itself by, and was dead at 29.
blurb: Hank Williams was born on 17 September 1923 in Mount Olive, a rural community in Butler County, Alabama. He was born with a spine condition, spina bifida occulta, that caused him pain all his life, and it was one reason he later drank heavily and took painkillers. As a boy he learned guitar from Rufus 'Tee Tot' Payne, a Black blues musician from Greenville, Alabama, and Payne and the country star Roy Acuff are named as the main influences on how he played and sang, so one of country music's founding figures learned from a Black bluesman. He started on local radio in Montgomery in the late 1930s with his band, the Drifting Cowboys. Fred Rose of Acuff-Rose signed him as a songwriter in 1946, and he joined MGM Records in 1947. His cover of 'Lovesick Blues' (1949) went to number one on the country chart and made him a star, and on 11 June 1949 he first played the Grand Ole Opry, country's most important radio show, and was called back for six encores. He also recorded spoken moral pieces as 'Luke the Drifter', so that jukebox operators would not mix them up with his honky-tonk records. The Opry fired him on 11 August 1952 for drinking and missing shows. His last session, on 23 September 1952, produced 'Your Cheatin' Heart' and 'Kaw-Liga', and he also wrote songs like 'Hey, Good Lookin''. He died on New Year's Day 1953, aged 29, when his heart failed in the back of a car near Oak Hill, West Virginia, after a doctor had injected him with vitamin B12 and morphine. Elvis Presley, Ray Charles, the Beatles, Bob Dylan, Johnny Cash and many others learned from his songs.
